desc:
A tiny markup language has elements of the form <NAME>content</NAME>. The rules are:

  • NAME is 1 to 9 uppercase letters, and the closing tag repeats the name of the opening tag exactly.
  • content may be empty. Otherwise it is a sequence of items, where each item is either a complete element or one plain character. A plain character is any character except < (so >, /, letters and digits are all fine as text).
  • A complete document is exactly one element: nothing may come before its opening tag or after its closing tag.

Return true if s is a valid document. For example <A></A>, <DIV>x<B>1</B>y</DIV> and <A>a>b/c</A> are valid. <A></B> (names differ), <A><B></A></B> (bad nesting), <A></A>x (text after the root), <A></A><B></B> (two roots), <a></a> (lowercase), <></> (empty name), <ABCDEFGHIJ></ABCDEFGHIJ> (10 letters) and <A><B</A> (a stray <) are not.
constraints: s contains letters, digits and the characters < > /; it has no spaces
hints: Opening and closing tags must nest properly, so think of a stack that holds the names of the elements that are currently open.
Whenever you see <, find the next > and look at the text in between: /NAME is a closing tag, NAME is an opening tag. Validate the name (1-9 uppercase letters) before using it.

The whole input must be a single root element: if the stack becomes empty before the end of the string, the document is valid only when that happened exactly at the last character; text or tags outside the root are invalid. Remember to reject a string that ends with elements still open.
editorial: Scan from the left with an index and a stack of open tag names. The string must start with <. At a <, locate the next > (if there is none, return false) and take the text between them. If it starts with / the tag is a closing tag and the name is the rest; otherwise it is an opening tag. A name is valid only if it has 1-9 characters, all uppercase letters; a name that contains a stray <, / or digit fails here. Push a name on an opening tag; on a closing tag the stack must be non-empty and its top must equal the name, which is then popped.

The single-root rule is checked at the moment the stack becomes empty after a pop: the closing tag has to end exactly at the last character, otherwise something follows the root and the document is invalid. Plain characters are allowed only while the stack is non-empty, which together with the requirement that the first character is < excludes text before the root. If the scan ends and the root never closed, return false.

Because the nesting can be tens of thousands of levels deep, use an explicit stack rather than recursion. Every character is read once, so the time is O(n) and the stack may hold O(n) names in total length.
